extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and natural philosophers studying classical celestial mechanics (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of propositions and problems from Newton's Principia (Section XI) concerning motion under centripetal forces, mutual attraction of bodies, methods to determine trajectories, times, and perturbative effects in multi-body systems. Includes demonstrations and corollaries illustrating orbital properties, isochronism, area-time relations, and approximations for many-body motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIII. Prob. XXXV. _Concessis figurarum curvilinearum Quadraturis, invenire vires quibus corpora in datis curvis lineis Oscillationes semper Isochronas peragent._
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the quadratures of curved figures, find the forces such that bodies moving in given curved lines always execute isochronous oscillations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: at a point T on curve STRQ, draw tangent TX and take TY equal to arc TR (using quadrature to know arc length). From Y draw YZ perpendicular to the tangent, and from C draw CT to meet YZ at Z; the centripetal force is proportional to TZ. Explanation: resolving the force into components TY and YZ shows YZ (parallel to the string) does not change the motion along the string while TY alters motion along the curve in proportion to the arc TR; hence equal parts yield simultaneous description of arcs and thus isochronous oscillations. Corollaries: (1) For a pendulum of length AT describing a circular arc, if an impressed machine force combines with gravity so total downward force is as arc TR to its sine TN, all single oscillation times are equal (isochronous). (2) In clocks, if machine-applied forces on the pendulum combine with gravity so that the total downward force is proportional to the rectangle of arc TR and radius AR to sine TN, then all oscillations are isochronous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIV. Prob. XXXVI. _Concessis figurarum curvilinearum quadraturis, invenire tempora quibus corpora vi qualibet centripeta in lineis quibuscunq; curvis in plano per centrum virium transeunte descriptis, descendent & ascendent._
rubrics_metrics.description: Given quadratures of curves and a law of centripetal force toward a center, find the times in which bodies descending and ascending along any given planar curve (which passes through the force center) traverse the curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: divide CS into equal parts, from each point draw circles centered at C cutting the curve in corresponding points. From Prop. XXXIX obtain velocity at any altitude CT. The time to traverse a small element Tt is proportional to its length and inversely to velocity; associate to each division an ordinate DN perpendicular to CS so that the rectangle Dd × DN (area DNnd) is proportional to time. By forming the curve SNn traced by the moving ordinate ends, the area SNDS is proportional to the time of descent along ST; hence from the area (given by quadrature) the time is obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LV. Theor. XIX. _Si corpus movetur in superficie quacunq; curva, cujus axis per centrum virium transit, & a corpore in axem demittatur perpendicularis, eiq; parallela & æqualis ab axis puncto quovis ducatur: dico quod parallela illa aream tempori proportionalem describet._
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body moves on any curved surface whose axis passes through the force center, and from the body a perpendicular to the axis is let fall and a line parallel and equal to it is drawn from any given point on the axis, that parallel describes an area proportional to time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up geometry: consider projections of the body's motion into a plane AOP by tracing the locus (vestigium) of the foot of the perpendicular. Resolve centripetal and normal forces; components perpendicular to AOP do not affect the projected motion. Thus the projected motion equals that of a body moving in the plane AOP under a centripetal force toward O equal to the sum of the resolved components; by Prop. I that yields that the sectoral area AOP described by radius OP is proportional to time. Corollary: same holds if bodies are attracted toward two or more centers on the same line: the projected area remains proportional to time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LVI. Prob. XXXVII. _Concessis figurarum curvilinearum Quadraturis, datisq; tum lege vis centripetæ ad centrum datum tendentis, tum superficie curva cujus axis per centrum illud transit; invenienda est Trajectoria quam corpus in eadem superficie describet, de loco dato, data cum velocitate versus plagam in superficie illa datam egressum._
rubrics_metrics.description: Given quadratures of curves, a law of centripetal force toward a given center, and a curved surface whose axis passes through that center, find the trajectory that a body describes on that surface from a given place with a given velocity directed toward a given point on the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: from the initial point S and given velocity determine velocity at other altitudes by Prop. XXXIX. For a small time interval the body describes a small arc Tt; construct the planar vestige Pp of that arc in a plane through O and the local tangent; draw a circle centered at T in the surface with radius Tt whose vestige is an ellipse PpQ in that plane. Given the area PO p proportional to time, one obtains the position Op and hence the intersection point p of the ellipse and line OP; iterating and erecting perpendiculars from vestige points gives successive trajectory points T. Thus the curve is obtained by successive geometric constructions using known quadratures and ellipse intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sect. XI introduction: De Motu Corporum Sphæricorum viribus centripetis se mutuo petentium
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory remarks: transition from bodies attracted to a fixed center to bodies mutually attracting; mutual attractions are equal and opposite (third law), so the center of gravity of a system either remains at rest or moves uniformly; treat centripetal forces as attractions (or impulses) for mathematical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that for mutual attractions one may consider centripetal forces toward the common center of gravity and proceed with mathematical reasoning, using familiar terminology and setting aside physical disputations. This frames the subsequent theorems about mutual attraction and relative motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LVII. Theor. XX. _Corpora duo se invicem trahentia describunt, & circum commune centrum gravitatis, & circum se mutuo, figuras similes._
rubrics_metrics.description: Two mutually attracting bodies describe similar figures both about their common center of gravity and about each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because distances to the common center are reciprocally proportional to the bodies (hence in a given ratio), and given equal angular motion about their own centers, straight lines in given ratios swept by equal angular motion trace similar figures. Therefore the figures traced about the mutual centers are similar. The proof relies on proportional distances and equal angular velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LVIII. Theor. XXI. _Si corpora duo viribus quibusvis se mutuo trahunt, & interea revolvuntur circa gravitatis centrum commune: dico quod figuris, quas corpora sic mota describunt circum se mutuo, potest figura similis & æqualis, circum corpus alterutrum immotum, viribus iisdem describi._
rubrics_metrics.description: If two bodies mutually attract and revolve about their common center of gravity, the figures they describe about each other can be identical and similar to the figures that would be described if one body were fixed and the same forces acted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct corresponding similar and equal curves traced by a point revolving about a fixed point and relate them to the mutual motion by parallel translations and similarity arguments. Two cases: (1) center at rest; (2) center moving uniformly in a straight line (which by Corollary 6 leaves relative motions unchanged). Hence the relative curve traced about an immobile point by the same forces is similar and equal to the mutual-motion curve. Corollaries: (1) Two bodies attracting with forces proportional to distance describe concentric ellipses. (2) If forces are inverse-square, they describe conic sections as before. (3) Radii drawn to the common center describe areas proportional to times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIX. Theor. XXII. _Corporum duorum S & P circa commune gravitatis centrum C revolventium tempus periodicum esse ad tempus periodicum corporis alterutrius P, circa alterum immotum S gyrantis & figuris quæ corpora circum se mutuo describunt figuram similem & æqualem describentis, in dimidiata ratione corporis alterius S, ad summam corporum S + P._
rubrics_metrics.description: For two bodies S and P revolving about their common center C, the periodic time is to the periodic time of the body P revolving about the fixed S (when S is immovable and the figure is similar and equal) as half the mass of the other body S is to the sum S+P (i.e., in the ratio of S to S+P, taken in a certain mean proportion fashion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From previous theorem the similar arcs are described in times proportional to distances; hence periods scale in the 'half' ratio corresponding to S : (S+P). Composing these ratios yields the period of the mutual system in terms of the single-body period about a fixed center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LX. Theor. XXIII. _Si corpora duo S & P, viribus quadrato distantiæ suæ reciproce proportionalibus se mutuo trahentia, revolvuntur circa gravitatis centrum commune: dico quod Ellipseos, quam corpus alterutrum P hoc motu circa alterum S describit, Axis transversus erit ad axem transversum Ellipseos, quam corpus idem P circa alterum quiescens S eodem tempore periodico describere posset, ut summa corporum duorum S + P ad primam duarum medie proportionalium inter hanc summam & corpus illud alterum S._
rubrics_metrics.description: For two bodies attracting by inverse-square forces and revolving about the common center, the transverse axis of the ellipse traced by P about moving S is to the transverse axis of the ellipse that P would trace about a fixed S in the same period, as the sum S+P is to the first of the two mean proportionals between S+P and S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses comparison of periods and how they scale with central attraction; if axes were equal the periods would differ in a ratio related to masses. Reducing period in that ratio changes the ellipse axis in a sesquiplicate ratio; manipulating these ratios yields the stated relation between transverse axes. The proposition links mutual-motion ellipse dimensions to single-body ellipse dimensions via mass-sum mean proportionalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXI. Theor. XXIV. _Si corpora duo viribus quibusvis se mutuo trahentia, neq; alias agitata vel impedita, quomodocunq; moveantur; motus eorum perinde se habebebunt ac si non traherent se mutuo, sed utrumq; a corpore tertio in communi gravitatis centro constituto viribus iisdem traheretur: Et Virium trahentium eadem erit Lex respectu distantiæ corporum a centro illo communi atq; respectu distantiæ totius inter corpora._
rubrics_metrics.description: If two bodies mutually attract by any forces and move (without other perturbations), their motion will be the same as if they were not mutually attracting but each attracted by a third body placed at the common center of gravity by the same forces; the law of attraction with respect to distance from that common center is the same as the law with respect to the mutual distance between the bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because forces tending to the bodies act toward them but can be regarded as tending to the intermediate center, the same laws with respect to distance hold when referred to the common center. Thus one may replace mutual attractions by attractions toward the center of gravity with corresponding distance-laws, enabling the reduction of mutual problems to single-center problems (useful for subsequent problems and theorems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXII. Prob. XXXVIII. _Corporum duorum quæ viribus quadrato distantiæ suæ reciproce proportionalibus se mutuo trahunt, ac de locis datis demittuntur, determinare motus._
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two bodies that attract each other by inverse-square forces and are released from given places, determine their motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Theorem LXI reduce the system to two bodies attracted toward the common center which is at rest by hypothesis; therefore motions are determined as in the single-center problems (Problem XXV). Thus one may determine the two-body motions as if each were attracted by the fixed central body at the center of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXIII. Prob. XXXIX. _Corporum duorum quæ viribus quadrato distantiæ suæ reciproce proportionalibus se mutuo trahunt, deq; locis datis, secundum datas rectas, datis cum velocitatibus exeunt, determinare motus._
rubrics_metrics.description: For two bodies attracting each other by inverse-square forces, given initial positions along specified lines and given initial velocities, determine their subsequent motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given initial motions, one can find the uniform motion of the common center, and by Corollaries reduce subsequent motions to those in the stationary space where the center is at rest; thus determine motion of each body through Problem IX and XXVI with corrections for the uniform progression of the system to obtain absolute motions in fixed space. The method composes the uniform center motion with the relative orbital motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXIV. Prob. XL. _Viribus quibus Corpora se mutuo trahunt crescentibus in simplici ratione distantiarum a centris: requiruntur motus plurium Corporum inter se._
rubrics_metrics.description: When the forces by which bodies mutually attract increase in simple proportion to their distances from the centers, determine the motions of multiple bodies among themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First treat two bodies with a common center, which describe ellipses with center at the common center. Add a third body S and resolve attractions into components; show that the pair T and L still describe ellipses (about their own centers) while S describes an ellipse about a new common center C, and the system can be generalized by adding more bodies. The argument shows that when mutual attractions scale simply with distance, the system's motions are obtainable by decomposition into elliptical motions about successive centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXV. Theor. XXV. _Corpora plura quorum vires decrescunt in duplicata ratione distantiarum ab eorundem centris, moveri posse inter se in Ellipsibus, & radiis ad umbilicos ductis Areas describere temporibus proportionales quam proxime._
rubrics_metrics.description: Many bodies whose forces decrease in the duplicate (square) ratio of distances from their centers can move among themselves in ellipses and, with radii drawn to umbilics, describe areas proportional to times, approximately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by considering limiting cases and approximations: (Case 1) many small bodies revolving around a much larger central body can be made arbitrarily small so that the central body remains practically at the center of gravity; the small bodies then move in ellipses and areas nearly proportional to times. (Case 2) consider a system of small bodies and one very large body moving together uniformly, and by taking large body distance sufficiently great the smaller bodies' mutual perturbations become negligible and they behave nearly as if orbiting a single mass. Corollaries discuss conditions and limits for approximating true motion by ideal ellipses and proportional area-time relations, and how errors can be made as small as desired by adjusting relative masses and distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXVI. Theor. XXVI. _Si corpora tria, quorum vires decrescunt in duplicata ratione distantiarum, se mutuo trahant, & attractiones acceleratrices binorum quorumcunq; in tertium sint inter se reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum; minora autem circa maximum in plano communi revolvantur: Dico quod interius circa intimum & maximum, radiis ad ipsum ductis, describet areas temporibus magis proportionales, & figuram ad formam Ellipseos umbilicum in concursu radiorum habentis magis accedentem, si corpus maximum his attractionibus agitetur, quam si maximum illud vel a minoribus non attractum quiescat, vel multo minus vel multo magis attractum aut multo minus aut multo magis agitetur._
rubrics_metrics.description: For three bodies with inverse-square attractions (and mutual accelerative attractions between any two relative to the third reciprocally as the square of distances), with smaller bodies revolving in a common plane around a large body, the inner body's areas (about the inner and maximum bodies) become more proportional to times and its orbit more closely approaches an ellipse with umbilic when the large body is itself set into motion by those attractions than when the large body is fixed or differently attracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed multi-case analysis: Case 1 (co-planar small bodies) and Case 2 (non-coplanar) show how additional attractions (resolved into components) perturb the orbit of a small body P about the large S. Introduce decompositions of third-body attractions into components along PS and parallel to QS and show how such components cause deviations from exact elliptical form and exact area-time proportionality. Main conclusions (corollaries): (1) inner body's motion is least perturbed when the large body S is attracted and moved proportionally by the others; (2) in three-body systems with exact inverse-square mutual attraction, body P describes areas faster near conjunction/opposition and slower near quadrature; (3) P moves faster in conjunction/opposition than in quadrature, (4) orbit curvature and radial excursions vary accordingly, (5) P recedes farther in quadratures than in syzygies, (6) central attraction changes produce variations in period and radius (leading to eccentricity changes), (7) apsidal line precesses (progresses or regresses) depending on perturbation sign and location, (8) apsidal motion depends on the deviation of central force from inverse-square between apsides, (9) if an additional perpetually increasing central force acts, eccentricity will grow, etc. The theorem formalizes many qualitative perturbation effects (conjunction/ quadrature asymmetries, apsidal motion, eccentricity evolution) and quantifies when the approximate elliptical and area-time relations hold best (when third-body perturbing components orthogonal or non‑proportional are minimal).
